title: Nothing audits whether a task's reward can be satisfied without the task being achieved
problem: I trust my suite's pass rate, but I have never checked whether a task can score as success while the goal state was never reached - so I do not know which direction my benchmark is wrong in.
symptom: A score that does not survive contact with users: the suite says 60% and the deployed agent behaves like 30%, or a genuinely capable agent scores below a compliant one. Re-auditing a handful of 'passed' transcripts turns up passes that achieved nothing.
why_now: Agentic rewards are written by hand, one per task, against an environment that the task author also wrote. A published 2025 audit of widely-used agentic benchmarks found reward defects large enough to move reported performance by up to 100% in relative terms, which means the defect class is normal rather than exceptional - and no standard artifact records that a reward was ever validated against the annotated end state.
existing: Human spot-checking of transcripts finds instances but produces no durable record that a task's reward was validated, so the audit is redone or skipped every release.
An LLM judge raises agreement with human judgement but is itself an unvalidated grader, so it moves the trust problem rather than closing it.
Comparing final database state against an annotated goal state is the strong form, but it exists per-benchmark rather than as a contract a harness enforces.

evidence.title: Establishing Best Practices for Building Rigorous Agentic Benchmarks
evidence.quote: For example, SWE-bench Verified uses insufficient test cases, while TAU-bench counts empty responses as successful.
evidence.note: Names the failure concretely in two of the most-cited agentic benchmarks: a reward that a no-op satisfies. The same abstract sizes the effect - 'Such issues can lead to under- or overestimation of agents' performance by up to 100% in relative terms' - and reports that applying their checklist to CVE-Bench 'reduces the performance overestimation by 33%'. Classified survey-aggregate because the paper synthesises a survey of practices and previously reported issues; the arXiv page I fetched (v5, 7 Aug 2025) shows no journal reference, so I am not claiming peer review.

evidence.title: An Illusion of Progress? Assessing the Current State of Web Agents
evidence.quote: Our results depict a very different picture of the competency of current agents, suggesting over-optimism in previously reported results. This gap can be attributed to shortcomings in existing benchmarks.
evidence.note: Peer-reviewed (the arXiv page carries the journal reference COLM 2025). Attributes the benchmark-to-real-task gap to the benchmarks themselves rather than to the agents, which is the claim this record's manual question is designed to force a team to test on its own suite. Date is the v4 submission date on the page I fetched.

evidence.title: Measuring the Impact of Early-2025 AI on Experienced Open-Source Developer Productivity
evidence.quote: Surprisingly, we find that allowing AI actually increases completion time by 19%--AI tooling slowed developers down.
evidence.note: The real-task end of the same gap, measured as an RCT on 246 tasks in mature repositories: the direction of the effect is opposite to what both the developers and expert forecasters predicted. Included because it establishes that the gap is not merely a scoring artifact - real-task outcomes can invert relative to expectations formed from benchmark-era capability claims. Classified practitioner-report: the arXiv page I fetched shows no journal reference.

build_hypothesis: A per-task reward validation record the harness can require: for each task, a stored no-op trajectory and a stored known-wrong trajectory, both asserted to FAIL, plus one known-good trajectory asserted to pass. A task with no such record is reported as unvalidated rather than counted in the score.

check.manual_question: Take three tasks from your suite at random. For each, can an empty or no-op agent response score as success? Does the reward compare the FINAL ENVIRONMENT STATE against an annotated goal state, or only the agent's own reported answer? Are the tests behind a pass sufficient to fail a plausible wrong solution? If you cannot answer for a task you did not write yourself, your pass rate has an unknown sign of error, not just an unknown magnitude.
check.rationale: Deliberately has NO present_when. Whether a reward can be satisfied without the goal being achieved is a property of the reward's semantics against its environment, and no lexical signature separates a sound grader from an exploitable one - a brittle regex here would manufacture verdicts on the one question in the register where a false ABSENT is most expensive. applies_when fires when the target owns graders or a task suite at all, so the finding is raised as MANUAL for exactly the projects that have something to audit.
